blocks.html: Three rules combine probabilities: the addition rule for “A or B” (§5.2.1), the multiplication rule for “A and B” (§5.2.2) and the complement rule for “not A” (§5.2.3). Each follows from the axioms in §5.1. They are not a complete toolkit on their own: combining events that overlap or influence each other needs extra information (a joint probability, a conditional probability, or an assumption of independence), and a fourth rule, the law of total probability, needs conditional probability and is derived in §5.3.

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: The addition rule gives the probability that at least one of two events occurs: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A and B).

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: Adding P(A) and P(B) counts the overlap, the outcomes where both happen, twice. Subtracting P(A and B) once removes the double count.

blocks.label: Derivation
blocks.html:
Split “A or B” into three pieces that share no outcomes: A only, B only, and both. By additivity (axiom 3):

P(A or B) = P(A only) + P(B only) + P(A and B).

A itself splits into “A only” and “both”, so P(A only) = P(A) − P(A and B). Likewise P(B only) = P(B) − P(A and B). Substituting:

P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) − 2P(A and B) + P(A and B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A and B).

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html: Among adults attending a PHC NCD clinic, P(diabetes) = 0.2, P(hypertension) = 0.3 and P(both) = 0.1. Then P(at least one) = 0.2 + 0.3 − 0.1 = 0.4, and P(neither) = 1 − 0.4 = 0.6. Without the overlap you would have claimed 0.5. Notice that the two single probabilities were not enough: the answer needed P(both).

points.html: When A and B are mutually exclusive (they cannot both happen, so P(A and B) = 0), the rule reduces to axiom 3: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B). A person’s ABO blood group being A and being B are mutually exclusive.
“Or” in probability is inclusive: “A or B” includes the case where both happen.
If P(A and B) is unknown, P(A or B) cannot be computed from P(A) and P(B) alone. You need the joint probability, or an assumption such as independence (§5.4), which supplies P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B).

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: The multiplication rule for independent events states that if A and B are independent (the occurrence of one does not change the probability of the other; made exact in §5.4), then P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B).

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: If a household’s water source tells you nothing about its size, then the share of households that have piped water and are large is the share with piped water times the share that is large. When one event does change the chance of the other, this simple product is wrong, and the general version (§5.3) replaces P(B) with the probability of B given that A has happened.

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html: In a CBHI household survey, P(piped water) = 0.6 and P(more than 5 members) = 0.3. If water source is independent of household size, P(piped water and more than 5 members) = 0.6 × 0.3 = 0.18. Whether that independence holds is a question to check in the data (a comparison of 0.18 with the observed joint proportion), not a fact to assume.

points.html: For independent events only: P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B). It extends to any number of independent events: P(A₁ and A₂ and … and Aₖ) = P(A₁) × P(A₂) × … × P(Aₖ).

The general form, valid with or without independence, is P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B|A), where P(B|A) is the probability of B given that A has happened, derived in §5.3 once conditional probability is defined.
Using the product for events that are not independent is a frequent error. Two children from the same household are not independent for diarrhoea: they share water, food and hygiene.

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: The complement rule states that the probability that A does not occur is P(not A) = 1 − P(A).

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: An event and its complement share no outcomes and together cover the whole sample space. So their probabilities add to 1. The rule’s real power is as a shortcut: when “at least one” is hard to calculate directly, calculate “none” and subtract from 1.

blocks.label: Derivation
blocks.html:
A and “not A” share no outcomes, and “A or not A” is the whole sample space S. By axioms 3 and 2:

P(A) + P(not A) = P(S) = 1, so P(not A) = 1 − P(A).

Because P(not A) ≥ 0 (axiom 1), it also follows that P(A) ≤ 1. This is the upper bound promised in §5.1.

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html: If P(a screening test is positive) = 0.15, then P(negative) = 1 − 0.15 = 0.85.

blocks.label: Worked Calculation: “at least one”
blocks.html:
A child has ten independent laboratory tests, each with probability 0.1 of an abnormal result.

  1. P(one test normal) = 1 − 0.1 = 0.9.
  2. P(all ten normal) = 0.9¹⁰ = 0.3487 (multiplication rule for independent events).
  3. P(at least one abnormal) = 1 − 0.3487 = 0.651.

Doing it directly would mean adding P(exactly 1), P(exactly 2), … , P(exactly 10); the complement needs one line.

points.html: P(not A) = 1 − P(A); equivalently P(A) + P(not A) = 1.
“At least one” = 1 − “none”. The pattern returns in the binomial distribution (§5.7.1.2) and in the family-wise error rate for multiple tests (§9.5.3).

blocks.label: Checkpoint 5.2

questions.prompt: A child has ten independent laboratory tests, each with a 5% chance of an abnormal result. What is the probability that at least one is abnormal? Show why the complement rule is the easier route.
questions.answer: P(one normal) = 0.95. P(all ten normal) = 0.95¹⁰ = 0.599. P(at least one abnormal) = 1 − 0.599 = 0.401. The direct route would add P(exactly 1) through P(exactly 10), ten separate calculations; the complement needs one.

questions.prompt: Two events are mutually exclusive. Explain, without using the word “exclusive”, why the addition rule simplifies for them.
questions.answer: They can never happen together, so no outcome belongs to both and P(A and B) = 0. There is no double-counted overlap to subtract, and P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B).

questions.prompt: P(A) = 0.2 and P(B) = 0.3, and A and B are independent. Find P(A or B).
questions.answer: Independence gives P(A and B) = 0.2 × 0.3 = 0.06. Then P(A or B) = 0.2 + 0.3 − 0.06 = 0.44.
